title: Encapsulation
summary: Hide an object's state behind methods so its rules cannot be broken from outside.

steps.title: The problem with public state
body: Here is an account anyone can ruin:
Every line of code in the program is now responsible for keeping the balance sensible. One mistake anywhere and the data is wrong, with no clue who did it.
**Access modifiers** decide who may touch a member:
- `private`: only code **inside the same class** can use it.
Members are `private` when you write no modifier at all. Private fields are usually named with a leading underscore.

steps.explain: `_balance` is private, so only code inside `Account` can touch it. The outside world has to go through `Deposit` and `GetBalance`.

steps.title: Private setters and invariants
body: A property can have a public `get` and a **private** `set`. Everyone can read it. Only the class can change it.
public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
Now `Withdraw` is the only door, and the door has a guard.

A rule that must always hold, like *the balance is never negative*, is called an **invariant**. Encapsulation means the class protects its own invariants, so the rest of the program cannot break them even by accident.
> **Tip:** `ArgumentException` says *the value you passed is wrong*. `InvalidOperationException` says *the value is fine, but the object is in no state to do this*.

steps.prompt: Outside code may read `Quantity` and call `Remove`, but must not set `Quantity` directly.
steps.explain: The setter is private, the method is public, and the method checks the rule before changing anything.

steps.prompt: This version returns `false` instead of throwing. What does it print?
code: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
steps.explain: The first withdrawal is refused and changes nothing. The second succeeds. The balance can only move through `Withdraw`, so it can never go below zero.

steps.title: Close the holes
prompt: This `Account` works, but anyone can put it into any state. Close the holes **without changing the names**.
1. `Owner` can only be set by the constructor.
2. `Balance` can be read by anyone but set only inside the class.
3. `Deposit` throws `ArgumentException` when `amount` is zero or negative.
4. `Withdraw` throws `ArgumentException` when `amount` is zero or negative, and `InvalidOperationException` when `amount` is more than the balance.
solution: public decimal Balance { get; private set; }
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
throw new ArgumentException("Amount must be positive");
template: Dojo.Eq("Owner comes from the constructor", "Maya", dojoA.Owner);
Dojo.Check("Owner cannot be set from outside", typeof(Account).GetProperty("Owner") is { } dojoOwner && dojoOwner.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "Owner should be a property with no public setter");
Dojo.Check("Balance cannot be set from outside", typeof(Account).GetProperty("Balance") is { } dojoBal && dojoBal.SetMethod?.IsPublic != true, "Balance should be a property with a private setter");
Dojo.Try("Withdraw(30) lowers Balance to 70", () => { dojoA.Withdraw(30m); Dojo.Eq("Withdraw(30) lowers Balance to 70", 70m, dojoA.Balance); });
Dojo.Eq("Balance is still 70 after the refused calls", 70m, dojoA.Balance);
Dojo.Try("Withdraw(70) can empty the account", () => { dojoA.Withdraw(70m); Dojo.Eq("Withdraw(70) can empty the account", 0m, dojoA.Balance); });
hints: Two of the fixes are in the property declarations: `{ get; }` and `{ get; private set; }`.
A guard is an `if` followed by `throw new ArgumentException("...");` at the top of the method.
In `Withdraw`, check `amount <= 0` first, then `amount > Balance` with `InvalidOperationException`. Only then subtract.

steps.title: The four access levels
body: `public` and `private` do most of the work. Two more exist:
| `internal` | any code in the same project |
| `protected` | this class and classes that inherit from it |
- A **class** written with no modifier is `internal`. That is fine for an app, and it matters when you write a library for other projects.
- A **member** written with no modifier is `private`.
- `protected` only makes sense with inheritance, which is two lessons away.
The habit to build: start with `private`, and open something up only when other code really needs it. It is easy to make a member public later. Taking it back breaks everyone who used it.

steps.title: readonly, and hiding collections
body: A `readonly` field can be assigned only where it is declared or in the constructor. After that it is locked.
throw new ArgumentException("Item name is required");
- `readonly` locks the **reference**. `_items` will always point at the same list, but the list itself can still grow.
- The list is `private`. If it were public, any code could call `cart.Items.Clear()` or add an empty name, walking straight past the check in `Add`.
So the cart exposes what callers need (`Count`, `Add`) and keeps the list to itself.

steps.prompt: Inside the `Cart` class, `_items` is declared `private readonly List<string> _items`. Which statement is true?
options: `_items.Add("Mug")` works, but `_items = new List<string>()` in a method does not compile
Both work, because `readonly` only affects code outside the class
steps.explain: `readonly` stops the field being pointed at a different list. It says nothing about what happens inside the list.

steps.title: A tag counter that cannot go wrong
prompt: Write a class `TagCounter` that counts tags and protects its counts. Your `Sk.Slug(text)` from First steps is ready: it turns `"Front End"` into `"front-end"`, so differently typed tags count as one.
- a **private readonly** `Dictionary<string, int>`;
- `void Add(string tag)`: counts `Sk.Slug(tag)`; a tag whose slug is empty is ignored;
- `int Count(string tag)`: the count of `Sk.Slug(tag)`, 0 if never added;
- `IReadOnlyDictionary<string, int> All`: every slug with its count, read-only for the outside.
`Add("Front End")` then `Add("front-end")` makes `Count("FRONT END")` 2.
template: Dojo.Eq("two spellings count as one tag", 2, dojoC.Count("FRONT END"));
Dojo.Check("no public fields", typeof(TagCounter).GetFields().Length == 0, "keep the dictionary private");
steps.explain: Outside code can read `All` but has no way to change a count except through `Add`: the counter's rule (one tag, one key) cannot be broken.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: the journal
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** The journal is where Sidekick keeps your tasks. Nothing outside it may touch the list directly, so it can never hold two tasks with the same title or two with the same id. Your `TaskItem` from the last lesson is ready to use.
Write a class `Journal`:
- a **private readonly** `List<TaskItem>` and a private next id that starts at 1;
- `IReadOnlyList<TaskItem> All`: the tasks, read-only;

- `TaskItem Add(string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)`: a title that matches an existing one (trimmed, ignoring case) throws `InvalidOperationException` with the message `"<existing title>" is already on your list.` (quotes included); otherwise creates `new TaskItem(nextId, title, estimateMinutes)`, adds it, then moves the next id on. A blank title fails in `TaskItem`'s constructor, so no id is used up;
- `void Restore(TaskItem task)`: puts back a task loaded from disk; a task whose id is already present throws `InvalidOperationException`; the next id moves past the restored id;
- `TaskItem? Find(int id)`: the task, or `null` (the `?` says *may be missing*);
- `bool Complete(int id)`: completes an open task and returns `true`; a missing or already done task returns `false`;
- `List<TaskItem> Open()`: a **new** list of the tasks that are not done.
solution: public TaskItem Add(string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
throw new InvalidOperationException($"\"{existing.Title}\" is already on your list.");
var task = new TaskItem(nextId, title, estimateMinutes);
if (Find(task.Id) is not null) throw new InvalidOperationException($"Task {task.Id} is already in the journal.");
if (task is null || task.Done) return false;
template: Dojo.Eq("the first task gets id 1", 1, dojoA.Id);
Dojo.Eq("the estimate is passed on", 45, dojoA.EstimateMinutes);
Dojo.Eq("the second task gets id 2", 2, dojoJ.Add("Write docs").Id);
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("a duplicate title is refused", () => dojoJ.Add(" FIX LOGIN "));
try { dojoJ.Add("fix login"); } catch (InvalidOperationException e) { Dojo.Eq("the message names the task", "\"Fix login\" is already on your list.", e.Message); }
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentException>("a blank title is refused by TaskItem", () => dojoJ.Add("   "));
Dojo.Eq("refused adds use up no id", 3, dojoJ.Add("Plan demo").Id);
Dojo.Eq("Find(99) is null", true, dojoJ.Find(99) is null);
Dojo.Eq("the task is done", true, dojoJ.Find(1)!.Done);
Dojo.Eq("Complete(1) again is false", false, dojoJ.Complete(1));
Dojo.Eq("Open leaves out done tasks", "Write docs,Plan demo", string.Join(",", dojoJ.Open().Select(t => t.Title)));
Dojo.Eq("clearing the list from Open() changes nothing", 2, dojoJ.Open().Count);
Dojo.Eq("Restore puts a task back", "Imported", dojoJ.Find(10)?.Title);
Dojo.Eq("the next id moves past a restored one", 11, dojoJ.Add("After import").Id);
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("restoring a used id is refused", () => dojoJ.Restore(new TaskItem(2, "Clash")));
Dojo.Check("no public fields", typeof(Journal).GetFields().Length == 0, "keep the list and the next id private");
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
hints: `Add`: loop over `tasks` and compare `existing.Title` with `title.Trim()` using `string.Equals(..., StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)`; throw with `$"\"{existing.Title}\" is already on your list."`.
Create the `TaskItem` **before** `nextId++`: if the constructor throws, the id is not used up.
`Find` loops and returns the match or `null`; `Complete` uses `Find`; `Open` builds a new `List<TaskItem>` of tasks with `!task.Done`.
steps.explain: `All` hands out an `IReadOnlyList`, `Open()` a fresh copy: callers can look at your tasks, but every change goes through `Add`, `Restore` and `Complete`, where the rules are.
